title: The Quark Hunt
summary: Zap electrons onto an oil drop one at a time until it hovers, calibrate a charge detector, and reject readings that are not whole electrons.
subject: physics
learningOutcome: After winning, the student can count the electrons on a balanced drop from n e V/d = m g, find the unit of charge from a set of readings, and reject a charge that is not a whole number of e.

levels.title: Hold the drop
levels.adds: Baseline: add electrons one at a time until n e V/d equals the drop's weight, so it hovers between the plates (q = n e, Ex 1.11a).
hints: The drop hovers when the upward push equals its weight: n e V / d = m g.
Solve for the number of electrons: n = m g d / (e V), with d = 0.005 m and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
n must come out a whole number. If the drop sinks it needs more electrons; if it rises, fewer.

levels.title: Calibrate the detector
levels.adds: New idea: the unit is not given. Find the largest step that every reading is a whole number of; the smallest reading need not be one unit.
hints: Every drop carries a whole number of electrons, so every reading is a whole number of the same step.
Look for the biggest step that goes into all three readings a whole number of times.
The smallest reading may be 2 or 3 electrons. Try dividing each reading by your step and look for whole numbers.

levels.title: Quark or dust?
levels.adds: New idea: with e known, reject every reading that is not a whole number of e, because free charge only comes as q = n e (Ex 1.4a).
hints: Divide each reading by 1.6: a real drop gives a whole number.
A result like 2.33 or 4.67 is a third of an electron off. No free charge like that has ever been found.
Flag every reading that is not whole, and only those, before you publish.

misconceptions: Charge can take any value at the atomic scale
The smallest measured charge must be the unit of charge
A reading a third of e away from a whole number is just noise
Adding one electron changes the force a little, so many counts could hover the drop
